Snapline 2.27.0

Two new annotation tools and a border for layers. Polygon draws triangles, stars and everything between from two numbers, with the seven named shapes a click away; Emoji stamps a glyph. A layer in the Editor's stack can now carry a border, and the Layers list is easier to work in.

Polygons and stars

  • A new Polygon tool (G) draws a polygon that fills the box you drag, said in two numbers: Sides, 3 to 12, and a Star slider that pulls the points in. One tool is therefore triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star and burst, and the Inspector names the shape you have. ⇧ while drawing squares the frame, and the rail button's glyph always shows the shape the next drag will put down.
  • Shape presets. The seven named shapes are offered by name: a Shape row in the Inspector above Sides and Star, a right-click on the rail's G button, or a press-and-hold on it. Applying one sets both numbers in one undo step and reshapes any selected polygons in place. The stepper and slider stay for fine-tuning.
  • It styles like a rectangle: colour, stroke width, opacity, a solid or dashed outline, and fill as none, solid, or a tint under the stroke. No corner radius and no rotation — a triangle points up.

Emoji stickers

  • A new Emoji tool (J) stamps a glyph with a click, sized by the stroke picker and resized afterwards by its corner handles. Pick from a grid of twenty-four in the Inspector, or type, paste, or choose any glyph from the system's Character Viewer. Picking another glyph swaps a selected sticker in place. A sticker takes opacity but no colour: the glyph carries its own.
  • Both are ordinary shapes: selected, moved, nudged, duplicated, reordered, deleted, and re-edited a week later, and each remembers its style between editors like every other tool.

Layers

  • Layer borders. With a layer selected, the Inspector's Stroke row — None, Thin, Medium, Thick — gives it a border, and a Color row appears once there is one: the palette, the eyedropper's sampled colours, or the system colour panel. The border draws just inside the layer's frame, so the frame stays the layer's whole footprint; it moves and resizes with the layer, fades with its opacity, and is baked into the export. Each change is one undo step.
  • The Layers list. A click on a layer's name selects it, as a click on its thumbnail did. Show, hide and lock live in the row alone — its eye and lock, its menu, and the canvas's — so the Inspector no longer repeats them as switches, and a selected layer's header names it on one line.

Fixed

  • A counter badge placed while Opacity was below full came out solid; stamps take the opacity now, as the Inspector said they would.
  • The Editor's window floor is taller, so the longer tool rail always shows every tool rather than cutting the last one off on a small capture.
  • Background's rounded corners with a shadow drew a black wedge into each corner of the preview at any zoom but 100 %: the canvas rounded on one arc and its shadow on another. Both now round on the canvas's own pixels. The exported file was never wrong.

Notes

  • The History index is now version 4, because a shape can be a polygon or an emoji. Versions before 2.27.0 cannot read the new file: on a downgrade, History appears empty and nothing is written. Upgrading again restores everything.
  • Privacy policy. The trial record Snapline's server keeps now also stores the two-letter country Cloudflare derived from the connection — a count of countries, nothing finer, never the IP address. The app sends nothing new and is told nothing.

Snapline 2.26.0

A layers release. The Editor's canvas is now a stack of pictures: drop images onto a capture and each lands where you let go, as a layer you move, resize, hide, lock, rename and fade, with its annotations following it. The canvas grows to make room — around an anchor, around every layer, or by pulling the crop frame past the edge. The Editor's Combine section becomes Arrange, a command over the layers you already placed. A capture that never grew a second layer is untouched: same file, same export, same History entry.

Layers

  • Drop images onto the canvas. Each file becomes a layer centred where it was dropped — shrunk to fit when it is larger than the canvas — topmost and selected under the Select tool, so the first drag places it. Add Images… in the Inspector's Layers section does the same from an Open panel. A card from History and a file from anywhere both work, and nothing is copied or filed: the layer borrows the file where it lives.
  • Move, resize, reorder. Drag a layer to move it; its eight handles resize it, ⇧ keeping the proportions. Arrow keys nudge a pixel, ⇧ ten. ⌘] and ⌘[ step it through the stack and ⌥⌘] and ⌥⌘[ take it to the top or bottom, as they do for shapes; the Layers list reorders by drag too. Every layer operation is one undo step with a name — Undo Move Layer, Undo Hide Layer — and ⌘Z after a move brings the picture back with its annotations.
  • Snap to guides. A moved layer's edges and middle take hold of the canvas's edges and middle and of every other visible layer's; a resize pulls only the dragged edge. Each line the layer sits on draws as a guide while the button is down. ⌘-drag moves free of the guides.
  • The Layers list. The Inspector's Layers section lists the stack topmost first, each with a thumbnail, its name, an eye and a lock; double-click or Return renames. The selected layer's opacity, visibility and lock sit at the top of the Inspector. A locked layer keeps its place and size while its annotations stay editable; a hidden one leaves the picture. ⌫ removes the selected layer with its annotations, and ⌘Z brings both back. The capture is the bottom layer and cannot be removed.
  • The capture is a layer too. Once a second layer exists, a click on the capture selects it; selected, it moves, resizes and nudges like any layer, its annotations with it. A drag on the unselected capture is still the marquee it always was, so composing on top of a screenshot never drags the screenshot out from under the pointer.
  • Annotations belong to the layer they were drawn on — the topmost picture under the shape — and move and scale with it, stroke and text size in proportion. A shape on empty canvas, or spanning two pictures, belongs to the canvas and stays put. Redaction, the eyedropper, Smart Redact, crop and every other tool work across the whole canvas, because the canvas is the image being edited.

The canvas

  • Canvas Size… (⌥⌘C) sets a width and height in pixels and holds the existing canvas to one of nine anchors; the new area takes the canvas colour. The new edge shows as an outline on the canvas and a diagram in the sheet as you type. Reveal All (⌥⌘R) grows the canvas to show every layer whole. Both live in the new Image menu and in the Inspector's Crop and Layers sections.
  • The crop frame grows the canvas. In the Crop tool the frame can be dragged past the picture's edge into the room around it. Applying it grows the canvas to enclose the frame first — one undo step, Grow Canvas — and then crops to the frame inside it; pull both sides out and you have a wider document, not a wider document with a crop on it. Zoom out for more room.
  • Arrange. The Combine composer's three layouts — side by side, stacked, grid — as a command over the stack, with a gutter and the canvas colour between. It positions the layers from their own sizes in stack order and never reorders the list. The canvas colour also fills empty canvas.
  • The status bar shows the dragged layer's position and size for the length of the drag, notes a canvas's new size after a change, and says Updating… while a slow rebuild runs; exports wait for it.
  • The stage around the canvas. A layer dragged past the canvas's edge keeps its outline and handles over the stage and can be grabbed, resized and right-clicked there. A click on the empty stage clears the selection, as a click on empty canvas does, and starts nothing.

Combine, in the Editor

  • The Combine section becomes Layers. A capture that stored a Combine arrangement opens with its tiling as layer frames, every annotation where it was, and its first save from this version writes the layers. The History grid's Combine — several captures into one new file — is unchanged.
  • What the stack can hold. Up to 12 layers including the capture, and a canvas — or a set of source images — up to 64 million pixels; a drop, a resize or a canvas change past that is refused with a note and changes nothing. A layer whose file has gone shows a gray placeholder and, while visible, blocks export by name: hide or remove it to export. The Quick Access card's Redact toggle asks for the Editor on a layered capture, as it did for a combined one.

Fixed

  • An image dragged over the Editor no longer stutters. The drop surface reads the drag once when it enters instead of asking the pasteboard and the disk on every pointer move.
  • The Editor's matte shows in Light Mode. The stage drew a white field behind the canvas, so a white capture had no visible edge; the grey matte now shows around the canvas in both appearances.
  • A crop dragged inward now takes on screen. The canvas view draws unclipped so a layer's outline and handles past its edge can show over the stage, and the cropped-away picture painted on around the smaller canvas: the crop applied but looked like it never took.

Notes

  • The History index is now version 3, because an entry can carry layers and a canvas, and a shape can name the layer it belongs to. Versions before 2.26.0 cannot read the new file: on a downgrade, History appears empty, nothing is written, and a copy is parked beside the index as history.unreadable.json. Upgrading again restores everything.

Snapline 2.25.0

A GIF release. Convert to GIF opens an options window: size, frame rate, speed, dithering and looping, three presets, a preview through the GIF's own palette, and an estimate of the file's size and conversion time before you convert. The one-click conversion is still there for anyone who prefers it.

Convert to GIF

  • Options before converting. The GIF button on a recording's card, and Convert to GIF… on a History tile or in the Shelf, open a Convert to GIF window. Size is Full (every pixel of the recording), Half, or a custom width — never upscaled past the source. Frame rate is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 fps; speed 1×, 1.5× or 2×; Dither gradients smooths shading and photos; Loop forever, or play once and stop on the last frame. Convert is the default button, so the remembered options cost one keypress. A second Convert on the same recording brings the window that is already up to the front.
  • Three presets. Chat (800 px, 10 fps — the GIF every earlier version made), Docs (half size, 15 fps) and Full (every pixel, 20 fps). Any other combination reads as Custom.
  • An estimate before the click. The window reads the recording once, runs ten short stretches of it through the real encoder, and quotes the file's size — with a range when the range is wide enough to matter — and how long the conversion will take, updating as you change the options. Past 10 MB it says so: GitHub and most chat apps won't play a GIF that large inline. Convert stays enabled either way. The preview is a mid-clip frame through the palette the GIF will actually hold, and the caption gives the output size, frame count and running time.
  • One click again, if you like. Untick "Show these options each time" and the GIF button converts straight away with the options you last used. Settings → Recording holds the same controls and turns the window back on.
  • Every frame rate keeps real time. A GIF's frame delays are whole hundredths of a second, so 15 or 30 fps cannot be one fixed delay. Snapline sets each frame's delay so that any run of frames sums exactly; a 10 s clip stays 10 s at every rate.
  • Dithering that keeps the file small. The dither is an ordered pattern keyed on the pixel's position, so a pixel that does not change between frames comes out the same in both and the still parts of a frame stay skipped, as before.

Fixed

  • A trimmed recording converts to its trimmed length. A recording trimmed to the middle of a keyframe group keeps the frames before the cut in the file, and the conversion used to schedule those frames as well, stretching the GIF past the trim.

Notes

  • The default GIF is byte for byte what 2.24 made: 800 px wide, 10 fps, looping, no dither. The 180 s limit on conversion is unchanged. Full size at 30 fps on a Retina recording can run to tens of megabytes — which is what the estimate is there to say before the click.

Show your clicks and keys in screen recordings

  • Highlight Clicks: every mouse click draws a brief expanding ring at the pointer — dual-tone, so it reads against any background. Display and region recordings.
  • Show Keystrokes: the keys you press appear in a capsule at the bottom of the movie, with shortcuts in the same ⌃⌥⇧⌘ symbols as the Shortcuts pane. Needs the Input Monitoring permission, asked once at the toggle; a recording never fails over it — refused access just means no capsule, and Snapline says so.
  • Both overlays are drawn into the recorded frames, so trims, GIF conversions, and shares keep them. The toggles live in the Record Screen bar and Settings → Recording, are remembered, and ship off. Worth knowing: Show Keystrokes records what you type — ordinary text included — into the video.

Snapline 2.16.0

Capture with Self-Timer: frame the region first, watch the countdown, and the shot fires by itself.

Capture

  • Capture with Self-Timer. Frame the region first, then a visible countdown runs — and the shot fires by itself. The delay is for staging: open the menu or tooltip you want inside the frame while the timer counts. Selection works exactly like a normal region capture (releasing the drag starts the timer — no extra confirm), and the countdown sits inside the region with the seconds, an Esc hint, and a ✕ to cancel. Nothing steals focus, so the menu you stage stays open, and the countdown never appears in the shot.
  • Pick 3, 5, or 10 seconds from the new status-menu item beside the Self-Timer setting — its top row remembers your last-used delay for a one-click repeat — or bind a shortcut in Settings → Shortcuts (it ships unbound). A canceled timer saves nothing and says so.
  • The invisible delay is gone. If you keep a sticky Self-Timer default set, region and main-display captures now show this same live countdown instead of silently stalling before the crosshair — same delay, visible and cancellable.

Snapline 2.15.0

History learns starred captures. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit.

History

  • History learns starred captures. Star anything worth keeping and it survives the retention sweep unconditionally — it never expires, and a starred card asks before a manual delete goes through. Star from the card's hover control or its Star/Unstar menu item; a starred capture wears a badge at rest. The History toolbar gains a Starred filter that combines with search.

Robustness

  • Fixed: Snapline could quit itself and not come back after you answered the Screen Recording prompt. The relaunch waited a fixed half-second before reopening, which could fire while the old copy was still shutting down — so nothing came back, and no crash report explained it. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit, and when it can't reopen safely it stays running and tells you instead of vanishing. The prompt for one permission no longer triggers a relaunch offer for another.
  • Also fixed: the camera bubble no longer scans for cameras on the main thread, which could stall the Record Screen bar (and probe for nearby iPhones) each time it opened; its window now closes cleanly instead of racing an in-flight animation; and the bubble's style controls no longer risk a crash from a settings change or a removed gradient stop.
